steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a systematization-of-knowledge paper on the security and privacy of human-centered wireless sensing: why wireless sensing matters, how it can be abused for inference attacks, the gap in existing surveys, and what our SoK contributes.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Wireless sensing: what it is and why it is growing
- Double-edged sword: benign applications vs. inference attacks
- Gap: no systematic understanding of attacks and defenses
- Our approach and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Wireless sensing: what it is and why it is growing
  - emerging enabling tech: smart homes/cities, autonomous systems, HCI
  - driven by advanced wireless comms (WiFi, 5G) + proliferation of devices (IoT)
  - signals (RF, light) interact with human bodies/objects -> variation reveals environment + human activities
  - example: Vasisht et al. -- localize/identify occupants from walking patterns -> smart home personalizes appliance settings
- Double-edged sword
  - benign: health status monitoring, energy-efficient smart home, friendly HCI
  - abuse: attacker infers private info -- location, living habits, behavioral biometrics (walking pattern, heart rate, hand gesture)
  - location -> location privacy leakage; living habits -> well-planned burglary; hand gesture to unlock phone -> password compromise
- Gap
  - literature lacks systematic understanding of inference attacks + defenses
  - existing surveys on wireless sensing focus on techniques + benign applications; privacy aspect largely untouched
  - hard to understand privacy vulnerabilities / design defenses; hard for engineers to build privacy-preserving systems
- Our approach and contributions
  - propose signal processing pipeline to systematize attacks/defenses
  - (1) taxonomy: generalized signal-processing-pipeline framework for reasoning about existing + future attacks/defenses
  - (2) open challenges: use framework to identify challenges, predict potential attacks, directions for defenses
  - (3) design space toward privacy-preserving sensing: core design aspects, design roadmap -- where/how private info leaks

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Wireless sensing is a new technology that enables a lot of applications, such as smart homes and smart cities, autonomous systems, and human-computer interaction. Because wireless communication techniques have become advanced (e.g., WiFi and 5G) and there are more and more wireless devices (e.g., Internet-of-Things), wireless sensing is getting more and more popular. Wireless signals come in different forms, including radio frequency (RF) and light, and when they are transmitted they interact with human bodies and other physical objects in the environment. Because of this, the variation of the wireless signals around a human can be used to understand the physical environment and the human activities in it. For example, Vasisht et al. show that wireless signals can be used to localize and identify the occupants of a home based on how they walk, so a smart home can know where the occupants are and who they are and personalize the appliance settings.

Wireless sensing is a double-edged sword, like almost any advanced technology. On one side, it enables many applications that improve quality of life, like health status monitoring, energy-efficient smart homes, and friendly human-computer interaction, by understanding the physical environment and what human subjects are doing. On the other side, an attacker can abuse the same technology to infer a human's private information, such as location, living habits, and behavioral biometric characteristics (e.g., walking pattern, heart rate, and hand gesture) that can identify a person, and this leads to privacy and security risks. For example, inferring location leads to location privacy leakage, inferring living habits can lead to well-planned burglary, and inferring the hand gesture used to unlock a smartphone leads to the password being compromised.

- Gap
  - literature lacks systematic understanding of inference attacks + defenses
  - existing surveys on wireless sensing focus on techniques + benign applications; privacy aspect largely untouched
  - hard to understand privacy vulnerabilities / design defenses; hard for engineers to build privacy-preserving systems
- Our approach and contributions
  - propose signal processing pipeline to systematize attacks/defenses
  - (1) taxonomy: generalized signal-processing-pipeline framework for reasoning about existing + future attacks/defenses
  - (2) open challenges: use framework to identify challenges, predict potential attacks, directions for defenses
  - (3) design space toward privacy-preserving sensing: core design aspects, design roadmap -- where/how private info leaks

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Wireless sensing is a new technology that enables a lot of applications, such as smart homes and smart cities, autonomous systems, and human-computer interaction. Because wireless communication techniques have become advanced (e.g., WiFi and 5G) and there are more and more wireless devices (e.g., Internet-of-Things), wireless sensing is getting more and more popular. Wireless signals come in different forms, including radio frequency (RF) and light, and when they are transmitted they interact with human bodies and other physical objects in the environment. Because of this, the variation of the wireless signals around a human can be used to understand the physical environment and the human activities in it. For example, Vasisht et al. show that wireless signals can be used to localize and identify the occupants of a home based on how they walk, so a smart home can know where the occupants are and who they are and personalize the appliance settings.

Wireless sensing is a double-edged sword, like almost any advanced technology. On one side, it enables many applications that improve quality of life, like health status monitoring, energy-efficient smart homes, and friendly human-computer interaction, by understanding the physical environment and what human subjects are doing. On the other side, an attacker can abuse the same technology to infer a human's private information, such as location, living habits, and behavioral biometric characteristics (e.g., walking pattern, heart rate, and hand gesture) that can identify a person, and this leads to privacy and security risks. For example, inferring location leads to location privacy leakage, inferring living habits can lead to well-planned burglary, and inferring the hand gesture used to unlock a smartphone leads to the password being compromised.

However, there is no systematic understanding in the literature of inference attacks via wireless sensing and of defenses against them. The existing literature surveys about wireless sensing focus on the sensing techniques and their benign applications, and they mostly leave the privacy side of wireless sensing untouched. Because of this gap it is hard to fully understand the privacy vulnerabilities of wireless sensing and to design effective defenses against inference attacks that may come in the future. Also, without a comprehensive systematization of wireless sensing systems, it is hard for engineers to design wireless sensing systems that preserve privacy.

This paper tries to bridge this gap. We propose a signal processing pipeline to systematize the inference attacks and defenses in human-centered wireless sensing systems. Our contributions are the following:

- Taxonomy of wireless signal processing in the inference attacks and defenses. Wireless signal processing is used a lot in human-centered wireless sensing systems for both inference attacks and defenses, so we propose a general framework based on a signal processing pipeline for reasoning about existing and future inference attacks and defenses.

- Open challenges. We use the framework we propose to identify important challenges for existing human-centered wireless sensing systems, to predict potential inference attacks, and to give directions for potential defenses against them.

- Identifying the design space towards privacy-preserving wireless sensing. We identify the core design aspects that future wireless sensing systems should take into account to be privacy-preserving, and we give a design roadmap by discussing where and how human private information has been leaked, based on our framework.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Wireless sensing is an emerging enabling technology for many applications such as smart homes/cities, autonomous systems, and human-computer interactions. With advanced wireless communication techniques (e.g., WiFi, and 5G) and the proliferation of wireless devices (e.g., Internet-of-Things), wireless sensing is becoming more and more popular. Wireless signals in different forms, including radio frequency (RF) and light, interact with human bodies and other physical objects in the environment during transmission. As a result, the variation of the wireless signals around a human can be leveraged to understand the physical environment and the human activities in it [1,2,3,4]. For instance, Vasisht et al. [3] show that wireless signals can be used to localize and identify occupants at home based on their walking patterns, which enables a smart home that knows the occupants' locations and identities to personalize appliance settings.

Like nearly any advanced technology, wireless sensing is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, wireless sensing enables many life-quality-improving applications such as health status monitoring [5,6,7], energy-efficient smart home [8,3,9], and friendly human-computer interaction [2,10] by understanding the physical environment and activities of human subjects. On the other hand, the same technology can be abused by an attacker to infer a human's private information such as location, living habits, and behavioral biometric characteristics (e.g., walking pattern, heart rate, and hand gesture) that can identify a person, leading to privacy and security risks. For instance, inferring location leads to location privacy leakage [3,11]; inferring living habits may lead to well-planned burglary [4,12]; and inferring the hand gesture used to unlock a smartphone leads to password compromise [13,14].

However, the literature lacks a systematic understanding of inference attacks via wireless sensing and of defenses against them. In particular, existing literature surveys about wireless sensing [15,16,17,18] focus on wireless sensing techniques and their benign applications, and largely leave the privacy aspect of wireless sensing unsystematized. This gap makes it hard to comprehensively understand the privacy vulnerabilities of wireless sensing and to design effective defenses against potential future inference attacks. Without a comprehensive systematization of wireless sensing systems, it is difficult for engineers to design privacy-preserving wireless sensing systems.

In this paper, we aim to bridge this gap. To do so, we propose a signal processing pipeline to systematize the inference attacks and defenses in human-centered wireless sensing systems. More specifically, we make the following contributions:

- Taxonomy of wireless signal processing in the inference attacks and defenses. Since wireless signal processing is extensively used in human-centered wireless sensing systems for inference attacks and defenses, we propose a generalized framework based on a signal processing pipeline for reasoning about existing and future inference attacks and defenses.

- Open challenges. We use our proposed framework to identify significant challenges facing existing human-centered wireless sensing systems, predict potential inference attacks, and provide directions for potential defenses against these attacks.

- Identifying the design space towards privacy-preserving wireless sensing. We identify the core design aspects that future wireless sensing systems should consider to achieve privacy-preserving properties, and provide a design roadmap by discussing, based on our proposed framework, where and how human private information has been leaked.
